articles.title: Argentina: NEA Flooding - DREF Operation (MDRAR026)
articles.description: Please refer to the attached file. Description of the Event Date of event 03-11-2026 What happened, where and when? Since 9 October 26, extraordinary rainfall has been recorded in the upper basin of the Paraná River, associated with the El Niño phenomenon. In the west of the state of Paraná (Brazil), more than 250 mm fell in 96 hours, and towards the end of October, new rains of up to 350 mm were recorded on the Iguazú basin and the Itaipu reservoir. This caused simultaneous flooding of the Iguazú, Paraná and Uruguay rivers. On October 14, the Iguazú River reached a flow of 16,200 m³/s, about eight times its average, and discharges from the Yacyretá dam reached about 35,000 m³/s. In Ayolas (Paraguay), upstream of the Argentine section, the Paraná River reached 6.43 m in October, the highest height for that month in 55 years. As of 19 October 2026, the Paraná River exceeded evacuation levels in Corrientes Capital, Itatí, Paso de la Patria, Barranqueras and Isla del Cerrito, and the flood wave advanced downstream towards Goya, Reconquista and La Paz. The number of displaced people went from 240 (16 October) to 2,296 (21 October) and to 4,190 as of 3 November 2026, according to the Argentine Red Cross's Situation Report No. 6: 2,239 in Chaco, 1,802 in Corrientes and 149 in Santa Fe, in 23 localities. Data consolidated by government authorities record 3,903 displaced people in 21 localities, of which 2,005 (51 per cent) are self-evacuated. In total, the authorities estimate that more than 5,028 people have been affected, 2 people have died (Bella Vista, Corrientes) and 1 person has been injured. In the Chaco, the impact is concentrated in the Gran Resistencia. Puerto Vilelas accounts for 60 per cent of the province's victims (1,350 people), followed by Colonia Benítez (450), Barranqueras (253) and Isla del Cerrito (142). Municipal records and the field survey of the Argentine Red Cross show a greater impact in Barranqueras. Isla del Cerrito continues to be isolated by land due to the closure of Provincial Route No. 63: essential transfers, health care and evacuations are made by boat. The internal and coastal roads of Colonia Benítez, Tres Bocas, Isla Soto and other places are disabled by flooding and mud. The catchment of the water treatment plants continues to be affected by camalots, turbidity and sediments, and the provincial water company maintains a restricted distribution or with reduced pressure at the peripheral points. In Corrientes, there are 1,802 displaced people in 12 coastal municipalities, of which 1,393 (77 per cent) are self-evacuated. The most affected localities are Corrientes Capital (672 people, in riverside neighborhoods such as La Tosquera), Itatí (518) and Paso de la Patria (228), where the rupture of an embankment affected more than 300 homes and pumping and containment work continues. In Santa Fe, the flood has already affected Las Toscas, Tacuarendí, Reconquista and Santa Fe Capital, with 149 people displaced. Although in recent days the river has registered decreases of a few centimeters in the upper section, the humanitarian impact does not improve: it is a pause within a scenario of prolonged high waters. As of 2 November 2026, the Paraná River marked 7.11 m in Corrientes (evacuation level: 7.00 m), after a peak of 7.35 m, and 7.00 m in Barranqueras (evacuation: 6.50 m). On 3 November, it dropped just 5 cm in Barranqueras. At that rate, the river will remain above evacuation levels for weeks and families will not be able to return to their homes. Meanwhile, the flood wave is advancing downstream: Goya (6.09 m) and Reconquista (5.91 m) exceed their evacuation levels, La Paz (5.86 m) exceeded the alert level, and the National Water Institute (INA) forecasts that Paraná and Santa Fe will reach or exceed the alert level in the second week of November. Added to this is the Paraguay River, which remains at 7.55 m, and the Bermejo River, which rose 18 cm on 3 November. The most worrying factor is the rain on an already saturated basin. For 3 to 4 November 2026, the National Meteorological Service (SMN) issued an orange alert for strong storms, some severe, throughout the province of Corrientes, with accumulated 40 to 80 mm and gusts of more than 90 km/h, and yellow alert in Chaco (20 to 40 mm), Misiones and Formosa. The Yacyretá Binational Entity forecasts between 2 and 4 November 2026 accumulated 20 to 50 mm in much of the Paraná basin, with up to 90 mm in some sectors. In southern Brazil, forecasts for November anticipate above-normal rainfall, with the highest excesses in the state of Paraná and risk of flooding over the unregulated basin of Alto Paraná and Iguazú. In Paraguay, rains and storms persist on the left bank of the Paraná and the Paraguay River basin, and the Paraná remains at 5.35 m in Ayolas, above alert and flood levels, with more than 3,200 people evacuated in that city alone. These figures are from a separate record and are not included in the displaced persons totals submitted for Argentina. As the soils have excess accumulated moisture, each new rain immediately drains into the rivers. That is why the National Water Institute (INA) warns that it is likely to observe new spikes and a second wave of flood in the Paraná River, due to the volume in transit from the Upper Paraná and the rains on the Paraguay River basin and the Itaipu contribution area, with a new flood transit from the Iguazú River. It also forecasts that the Uruguay River will approach the alert level again in São Tomé and San Javier between 6 and 8 November 2026. The Yacyretá Binational Entity also anticipates a new increase in flow after the current slight decrease. On a seasonal scale, the SMN forecasts above-normal rainfall on the Littoral for the November–January quarter. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center anticipates a strong to very strong El Niño, with a high probability of reaching historic intensity and persisting at least until the January–March 2027 quarter. In this context, an increase in hydrometeorological events (intense rains, severe storms, and floods) is expected until February–March 2027 throughout the La Plata Basin, including the Uruguay River and the Paraná Delta. The Civil Defense Directorate of Corrientes describes a long-term emergency, until March or April 2027, and the Government of Chaco estimates stays of 3 to 4 months in evacuation centers. With this scenario, some 200 additional families are projected to be affected (around 1,000 people) in the prioritized areas in the coming weeks, in addition to possible new effects in Santa Fe, Entre Ríos, and Buenos Aires. Exceptional nature of the event. The magnitude of this flood is exceptional for the basin and, according to official forecasts, the situation has not yet reached its peak. Upstream, the Paraná River in Ciudad del Este (Paraguay) marked the historical maximum of its series of records (32.96 m, on 15 October 2026), and the stations of Cerrito, Panchito López and Itá Corá surpassed their records of November 2023. In Ayolas, the October height was the highest in 55 years. The Iguazú River reached about 17,700 m³/s on 26 October, almost 12 times its average flow, and the Devil's Throat was closed for 20 days. The flows entering Yacyretá, of about 35,000 m³/s, are equivalent to 2.4 times the historical average of October (14,400 m³/s, series 1971–2025). In Corrientes and Barranqueras the river has remained above the evacuation level since 19 October. The most worrying thing is not the current reading but what is coming: the INA and the Yacyretá Binational Entity predict new rebounds, a second wave of floods and new increases in flow due to the rains expected over a saturated basin in northern Argentina, southern Brazil and Paraguay. Added to this is an El Niño with a high probability of reaching historic intensity, which would sustain high waters until February-March 2027, in the middle of the dengue season. To date there is no declaration of national or provincial emergency. The National System for Integrated Risk Management (SINAGIR) maintains the Red Alert for the region. The Chaco alert system maintains the red alert in Barranqueras, Puerto Vilelas and Isla del Cerrito, and in Corrientes there are 11 coastal municipalities on alert. Reconquista (Santa Fe) has a municipal emergency, and on 31 October 2026 a bill to declare a water emergency in the Chaco entered the Senate of the Nation, which has not yet been discussed.
